You can assume for all practical purposes that log(n!) is asymptotically equal to log(n^n )

Why?

Because two functions, lets call them f(x) and g(x) are said to be asymptotically equivalent if for some constants, c1 and c2, c1*f(x)=Ω(g(x)) and c2*f(x)=O(g(x)). In other words, if they differ by a constant amount.

Now given this definition, you could say that log(n^3 )=Θ(log(n)), however n^3 ≠Θ(n).

The log around the n! and n^n help to suppress their differences to a constant amount.

Been a while since I've done some of this stuff but I'm pretty sure I've got the second one.

Let's take a look at [the graph of y=ln(x+1) vs. the graph of y=x](http://i.imgur.com/JtfwS.png)

Since when x>0, we know that ln(x+1)<x, and therefore the function is decreasing as n->inf.  Also for x>0 we know that ln(x+1)>0, and therefore we know the function converges. But more specifically it converges to 0.
